passages.t: Freed at Ramah, and Jeremiah chooses to stay
passages.happening:
The word came to Jeremiah after Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, had released him at Ramah, where he had been found in chains among the captives of Jerusalem and Judah being taken to Babylon (verse 1).

The captain tells Jeremiah that the LORD his God decreed this disaster on this place and has done what he said, because the people sinned against the LORD and did not obey him (verses 2 and 3). Now he frees him from the chains on his wrists. If Jeremiah wants to come to Babylon, he will look after him; if not, he may stay. The whole land is before him; he may go wherever he thinks good (verse 4). Before Jeremiah turns to go, Nebuzaradan adds that he may return to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon has made governor over the towns of Judah, and live with him among the people, or go anywhere else he likes. He gives him food and a gift and lets him go (verse 5).

‘So Jeremiah went to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah and stayed with him among the people who were left in the land’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 adds what chapter 39 did not say. Jeremiah was first swept up in chains with the other captives and taken to Ramah, a town a few miles north of Jerusalem that served as a gathering point for deportees. There Nebuzaradan recognized and released him. The two accounts are usually read together, with chapter 39 summarizing and chapter 40 filling in.

It can seem strange for a foreign officer to speak like a prophet of Israel. Some scholars think the narrator shaped his words to express the book's message. Others note that conquerors in the ancient world often claimed that a defeated city's own god had abandoned it; an Assyrian officer said much the same outside Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day. Nebuzaradan may also have known Jeremiah's message, which had been public for years.

Jeremiah was offered comfort in Babylon. He chose to stay with the poor in the ruined land.
passages.later: Kings records the appointment: ‘Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, over the people he had left behind’ (2 Kings 25:22). An Assyrian officer had once claimed that the LORD himself sent him against Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:25).
passages.asks: Jeremiah could have gone to Babylon in comfort and chose to stay among the poor. Ask where you are offered comfort at the cost of leaving people who need you. And ask what it means that even a foreign officer could see what God had done.

passages.t: Gedaliah governs at Mizpah, and a warning ignored
passages.happening:
When the army commanders still in the field hear that Gedaliah has been made governor over the poor who were not taken to Babylon (verse 7), they come to him at Mizpah: Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan and Jonathan sons of Kareah, and others (verse 8). Gedaliah swears to them not to be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. They should live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with them (verse 9). He will stand for them before the Chaldeans, and they are to gather wine, summer fruit and oil and live in their towns (verse 10).

The Judeans in Moab, Ammon, Edom and other lands hear of it and come back to Gedaliah at Mizpah (verses 11 and 12). ‘And they gathered an abundance of wine grapes and summer fruit’ (verse 12).

Johanan son of Kareah and the commanders warn Gedaliah that Baalis, king of the Ammonites, has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to kill him. Gedaliah does not believe them (verses 13 and 14). Johanan offers privately to kill Ishmael before he can strike, so that the remnant of Judah will not be scattered (verse 15). Gedaliah forbids it and says what Johanan says about Ishmael is a lie (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Gedaliah came from the family of Shaphan, royal scribes who had supported Jeremiah for decades. His appointment made Mizpah the center of what was left of Judah. Mizpah is usually identified with Tell en-Nasbeh, about eight miles north of Jerusalem, where excavations suggest the town went on being lived in rather than destroyed.

For a moment there was hope. Scattered Judeans came home, and they gathered a rich harvest from the abandoned fields and vineyards.

Gedaliah was trusting and honorable, and he refused to approve a killing on suspicion. But the warning was true, as the next chapter shows. His goodness left him open to a man who meant him harm.
passages.later: Kings tells the same story in brief: ‘Do not be afraid of the servants of the Chaldeans. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon’ (2 Kings 25:24). Proverbs says, ‘The prudent see danger and take cover’ (Proverbs 22:3).
passages.asks: Gedaliah would not believe a warning about a man he trusted. Ask how you hold together trust in people and wisdom about danger. And ask what harvest God may still give in a place that looks ruined.
